solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: False promises to pay following prompt (8)

indicators.note: something following comes after, so the promises to pay are written after the prompt

blocks.note: to spur someone on is to prompt them
an IOU ('I owe you') is a written promise to pay

annotation.surface: Someone is cynical about pledges of payment that only arrive after a reminder.
annotation.walkthrough: 'False promises' looks like one phrase; the definition is 'False' alone, and 'promises to pay' is the plural IOUS.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a claim that is fake or not genuine is both false and spurious.

clue.text: In favour of cool European being blasphemous (7)

blocks.note: to fan something is to cool it

annotation.surface: Someone approves of a laid-back European whose language is irreverent.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cool' reads as an adjective praising the European; it is the verb, as when you wave a fan to cool yourself.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: language that shows contempt for sacred things is both profane and blasphemous.

blocks.note: OT = Old Testament, the crossword's usual 'books'

annotation.surface: A thief looting books in exchange for a machine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Books' as OT (Old Testament) or NT is a convention worth learning early.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a machine that moves and acts by itself is an automaton.

indicators.note: whatever is held by something sits in its grasp, so the answer sits inside the words that follow

blocks.note: majOR Benefactor, spanning the gap between the words

annotation.surface: A globe gripped by a wealthy patron, like a monarch in a portrait.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer straddles two words, which is why it is easy to read past.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, best known from the jewelled globe a monarch holds at a coronation.

indicators.note: something manufactured is made out of raw materials, so the letters of MALTS EARL are made into something new

annotation.surface: An aristocrat is suspected of producing his own malt whisky.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Suspect' reads as an adjective for the malts; it is the definition, a verb.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: sensing that something underhand is going on is to suspect it.

indicators.note: to remove something is to take it away, so the L is taken out
names the word the L is taken out of, the one for 'cut'

annotation.surface: An instruction for tailoring: unpick a line of stitching from a trimmed belt.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut belt' looks like one thing; 'cut' is the word losing its L and 'belt' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a band of cloth tied round the waist is a kind of belt.

clue.text: Fully gratify one entering gallery following special arrangement initially (7)

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so take the first letters of 'special arrangement'
something entering a building goes inside it, so I goes into the gallery TATE
something following comes after, so the gallery part is written after S and A

blocks.note: the Tate, the London art gallery
I = one, the Roman numeral; it enters TATE after the T

annotation.surface: A satisfied visitor enters a gallery after a special exhibition has been arranged.
annotation.walkthrough: The Tate is Britain's national gallery of British and modern art, the crossword's favourite gallery.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to fill someone's appetite completely is to fully gratify it.

blocks.note: a person from one particular Scandinavian country
a yellow-fleshed root, called rutabaga in America

annotation.surface: A description of a Scandinavian vegetable.
annotation.walkthrough: Read as one phrase it describes a Nordic vegetable; the swede is simply the British name for a rutabaga, and a Swede is someone from Sweden.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: a native of Sweden, and the vegetable once called the Swedish turnip.

indicators.note: a horse biting something closes its mouth round it, so COB closes round M

blocks.note: a cob is a sturdy short-legged horse
M = male; it goes inside COB

annotation.surface: A horse bites the man who looks after it in the stable.
annotation.walkthrough: In the stable scene 'groom' is a stable hand; here it is the verb, to tidy hair or a coat.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: running teeth through hair or a horse's coat grooms it.

blocks.note: anyone alive draws breath, read literally
a short pause to get your breath back

annotation.surface: A description of an idler who lives only for relaxing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lives for rest' sounds like a lazy person; split after 'lives' and there are two separate senses.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: literally someone who breathes, so is alive, and idiomatically a short break.

blocks.note: an oral is a spoken exam

annotation.surface: An old exam once used to decide nationality.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Country' looks like a nation; it is the adjective, as in country life.
annotation.definitionFit: Adjective for adjective: shepherds' and rural scenes are pastoral, of the country.

clue.text: Prudence about to pull head of technology (9)

indicators.note: the head of anything is its top, so take the first letter of 'technology'

blocks.note: to strain is to pull hard

annotation.surface: A woman called Prudence is about to sack the company's head of technology.
annotation.walkthrough: Prudence reads as a woman's name and 'about to' as 'on the point of'; the phrase splits, with 'about' and 'to pull' as separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: careful self-control and caution are prudence.

indicators.note: something flipped is turned over, so REV is turned round to VER

annotation.surface: A clergyman lost his temper and started cursing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flipped' suits a vicar losing his temper, and 'Swear' suggests bad language; here it means to state solemnly.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of declaring firmly that something is true.

annotation.surface: Footwear decorated with tassels.
annotation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like a link word joining the parts; it supplies a letter.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: shoes with a solid wedge-shaped sole and heel.

clue.text: Sugar bag emptied partly in rubbish (7)

indicators.note: only part of the phrase is used, the run of letters inside 'sugar bag emptied'

annotation.surface: An empty sugar bag thrown partly into the bin.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Emptied' tempts you to drop the insides of a word; it only supplies the final E.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, the American word for household rubbish.

indicators.note: without a heart means without its centre, so REFEREE loses its middle letter
something crushed is squashed out of shape, so the letters are pressed into a new order

annotation.surface: A callous match official stubs out a cigarette.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crushed' fits stubbing out a cigarette, but here it scrambles the letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a cannabis cigarette, in old slang.

indicators.note: whoever is drinking takes the drink inside, so ELATE takes EV inside it
at regular intervals, so take every other letter of 'bevvy'

blocks.note: bEvVy, second and fourth letters; they go inside ELATE

annotation.surface: A drinking toast: raise a glass and cheer while having a drink.
annotation.walkthrough: A bevvy is British slang for an alcoholic drink, which keeps the pub scene going.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to lift something higher.

indicators.note: with its end taken away, the vegetable drops its last letter

blocks.note: a leafy green related to beetroot; it loses its final D

annotation.surface: A cook burns a vegetable after trimming off its end.
annotation.walkthrough: Chard is a leafy green vegetable; the surface has it trimmed and burnt.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to burn the surface of something black.

indicators.note: words that are chanted are heard rather than read, so go by the sound

blocks.note: a hoard is a stockpile, a store

annotation.surface: A crowd of shoppers inside a shop singing together.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Store' reads as a shop, the place the crowd is in; it is a stockpile.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a large, unruly crowd.

clue.text: Dental appliance trainee fixed after run (8)

indicators.note: something fixed has been repaired, put back together, so TRAINEE is reassembled in a new order
the rearranged trainee comes after the R

blocks.note: R = run, as on a cricket scoreboard

annotation.surface: A junior dentist fitted a brace after a run of appointments.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fixed' suits a dental appliance being fitted; it is the rearranging instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a brace worn to hold teeth in place after orthodontic work.

clue.text: Small bay trees primarily found south of popular lake’s edges (5)

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so take the first letter of 'trees'
south is below on a map, and in a down answer the T sits below the rest
a lake's edges are its outside, so take the first and last letters of 'lake'

annotation.surface: Trees growing mainly on the south side of a popular lake, near a bay.
annotation.walkthrough: 'South of' means below, which only works in a down clue.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a narrow arm of water running into the land.

clue.text: Getting cold feet about daughter studying (8)

blocks.note: D = daughter, as in family trees
to read a subject is to study it at university

annotation.surface: A parent is nervous about a daughter going off to university.
annotation.walkthrough: 'About' looks like a container instruction; it belongs to the definition, 'getting cold feet about'.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: to get cold feet about something is to lose nerve and fear it.

clue.text: Band’s performance going up and down (3)

indicators.note: a word reading the same going up the grid as going down it is a palindrome

blocks.note: palindrome indicator: the three letters read identically in either direction

annotation.surface: A band plays a lively set, with the crowd jumping up and down.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition names the word; 'going up and down' says it reads the same either way in this down entry.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a single live booking for a band or musician.

indicators.note: something destroyed is broken up, so the letters of FLEA are broken and reassembled

annotation.surface: A pest is destroyed after damaging a plant.
annotation.walkthrough: It reads as a flea being killed; 'destroyed' is the instruction to rearrange FLEA.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example: one part of a plant, alongside stem and root.

indicators.note: at regular intervals, so take every other letter of 'shoetree'

annotation.surface: A note saying the shoetree is always kept in the same spot.
annotation.walkthrough: A shoetree is a shoe-shaped block kept inside a shoe to hold its shape.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the adverb of place.

clue.text: Time and love make that woman well-organised (8)

blocks.note: love = zero in tennis, so O
to make a train is to get it

annotation.surface: Time and love turn a woman into someone who has her life in order.
annotation.walkthrough: The informal adjective describes a person who is calm and has their life in order.
annotation.definitionFit: An informal sense: someone composed and on top of things is well-organised.
